title: Concepts
text: You ask, and Ringkeeper does the work for the right client. That's the whole app: agents and routines are extras, for work that should start without you. Once these eight ideas click, the rest follows. **Request.** What you ask, in your own words: typed or spoken, in the app or on Telegram. It starts a conversation, and this is how nearly everything begins. **Client.** Someone you do work for, like General Informatics LLC. Each client's projects and connections are kept apart from every other client's: a task for one client can never reach another client's data. **Project.** One piece of a client's work: a website, an app, a set of automations. Every request goes to one project, and its task works in that project's folder. A project has other names people use ("the geninfos site"), so Ringkeeper can tell which one you mean. **Connection.** A client's service that their projects can use: a database, Airtable, n8n, Vercel, GitHub, a Google account, Twilio, an MCP server. Ringkeeper keeps the key in its vault and makes each call itself; the AI never sees a key. A connection is marked production, staging or development. **Shared tool.** A tool of yours that holds no client's data, like a web browser or files on this computer. You can give it to any client's projects, or to all of them. **Agent.** Optional. A named helper inside one project, with instructions it always follows and only the connections you give it. *An agent is who does the work.* **Routine.** Optional. When an agent runs on its own: on a schedule, when something happens (an email, a file, a webhook), or when you press Run. *A routine is when it runs.* **Hold.** A change to live client data (a production connection), or anything that reaches real people (an email, a text), waits for your OK in Approvals. Nothing happens until you approve it, and everything is logged.

title: A request, start to finish
text: 1. You ask, in plain words: "Add last week's leads to General Informatics' Airtable." 2. Ringkeeper picks the project (it asks if it isn't sure) and starts a task. 3. The task reads what it needs through the project's connections. 4. A change to production is held. You see exactly what would run, and approve or deny it. 5. The task goes on with the result and reports back in the conversation. Most data changes can be undone for 7 days (what can and can't). A task that couldn't do what you asked ends as **Not done**, never Done, and says why: on its card, on its page, and in the chat you asked from. When what it lacked is a connection the client has but the project isn't linked to, it offers one click, like "Link General Informatics' Google to Website and retry", in the app and as a button in the chat. A task does all its work before it answers: nothing of it runs in the background or after it ends, so an answer never says the rest is still being fetched.

title: A task's changes to files
text: A task that works on a project's code (a feature, a fix, content) works on a branch of its own, and leaves the folder checked out as it found it. To use the changes, open the task's **Changes** tab: **Keep these changes** merges them into the project's main branch, and **Discard** throws them away. A follow-up in the same conversation keeps working on the same branch, so it sees the earlier work. A task that only read changes nothing and leaves no branch. One code task works in a project's folder at a time; another waits until it's done. If the folder has edits you haven't committed, a code task doesn't start and says so: commit or stash them first. Only the files the task itself edited go on its branch. A file someone else edited during the run stays out, and the task names it. After a command the task ran, it can't tell who edited what, so every edited file goes on the branch and the task names the ones it didn't edit itself. Work with data or connections, and general work like a web lookup, doesn't use git at all: no branch, no waiting for the folder, and uncommitted edits don't stop it. If such a task does write files in the folder, its page says so ("Changed 2 files in the folder, not on a branch").

title: Files a task makes
text: The files a task made or changed are listed on its page (the **Changes** tab) and under its result in the conversation. In the desktop app each has **Open** and **Show in folder**. A code task's files are on its branch until you keep them: they open from a copy, and your folder isn't touched. Only documents open: PDFs, Office files, text, Markdown, CSV, JSON and pictures. Anything else (a program, a script, a web page) is only shown in its folder, so nothing a task wrote runs by a click. A table in a result has **Copy** (to paste into a spreadsheet) and **Download CSV**. In the desktop app the CSV is saved in your Downloads folder (as `table.csv`, or `table (2).csv` when that's taken; nothing is overwritten), and **Show in folder** shows it there.

title: Where a request goes
text: The client and project chosen at the top of the app are a firm choice for new requests, like an @-mention: the box says "Sending to Alexey › My Project", and a request sent then goes to that project without asking. Two exceptions: an @-mention of another project or client in the request wins, and when the request is clearly for another client's project, it asks once ("This looks like it's for Acme, but My Project is selected"), with both as buttons. Work that needs no client's connection, like a web lookup, writing, or summarizing text you pasted, runs in the chosen project. With nothing chosen, it runs in your own client's default project: on that client's page, open **Settings › Your own work** and turn on "... is me". A follow-up stays where its conversation's work is. Once a conversation has a task in a project, a later message there that names no other project, client or connection runs in the same project, even if it needs no connection ("Thanks. Now say that again in two sentences"). Whether a project's tasks can use the web is its own setting (the project's Settings tab, **Web access**), apart from how independently it works. Left at the default, it's on for your own client's projects and off for a client's, so their data doesn't leave unless you allow it. A request that needs the web in a project where it's off says so and asks once, with **Allow web for this project and retry** (in the app and in your chats). A question about your setup ("how many connections do we have?") is answered from Ringkeeper's own records, without a project. A request that names a connection and asks to use or read it ("Use Demo CRM to list the tools it offers") is always a task in a project linked to that connection, even when it asks what the connection can do. Asking where a connection is linked, or whether its token is about to expire, is still a question about your setup.

title: When it asks which project
text: Ringkeeper asks only when the work clearly belongs to one project and more than one fits, and says why in one line, like "Both Website and Blog have a contact form." A request that names a client but none of its projects, for work on one project's own things ("add a file to Acme's project folder"), is always asked about when the client has more than one. It doesn't ask: - **With one option.** If only one project could be meant, the work goes there. - **Again in the same conversation.** Once you've picked, later requests there go to the same project unless they name another. - **For work any of a client's projects would do**, like reading their email or Google. That goes to the client's **default project**: their only project, or the one you choose on the client's Overview tab. The first time it would have asked, the question offers to make your pick the default. You can answer by replying, too, in the app or a chat: send just the project's name ("Blog", "the Acme one", "Alexey, My Project") right after the question, and the request you sent runs there, with no second question. A project's own name wins over another project's nickname that's part of it: "Demo site" means Demo site, even if Demo shop is also called "demo". The same request sent again while it's still running doesn't start it twice: the reply says it's already working on that, with a link. "None" or "neither" starts nothing. When it asks to go ahead on production, "yes" or "do it" is the go-ahead. If it said it couldn't tell where a request goes, a reply that's just the project's name sends that request there. Only a reply that's just a name, sent right after, counts as the answer. A message that asks for something ("List Acme's active workflows") is a new request even if it names a project, and the question stays open. Other short follow-ups, like "use my own Google instead", continue the open request. See also: Connections, Agents and routines, Approvals and safety.

title: Connections and shared tools
text: A **connection** is one client's service: their database, Airtable base, n8n, Vercel, GitHub, Google account, Twilio number, or an MCP server. You add it once, link it to that client's projects, and every task in those projects can use it. A connection can't be linked to another client's project. A **shared tool** is yours, not a client's: a web browser, files on this computer, a search tool. It holds no client data, so it can go to any project, or to all of them (new ones too), with exceptions. You're asked right after adding one.

title: Adding one
text: **Connectors › Browse connectors** (or a client's Connections tab, or press Ctrl+K and type "add a connection"). It asks first whether it's a client's account or your own tool. Built-in services come first, each a tile that opens its form; then the services you sign in to; then **Other connectors**, a search of every MCP server, with the service's own first and community servers folded away. The form links to the page where the service gives you its key. Tiles are grouped by what they're for: CRM, Accounting, Payments, CMS and so on. Some vendors sign in through an app of your own: see Developer apps. Using these in Claude? Claude's connectors stay in your Claude account; connect them here once per client. - **Is this live client data?** Asked every time, with no default. Production is live data: every change on it waits for your approval. On staging and test data, a built-in service's changes run straight away, and are logged (texts and emails still wait). - **Its name** reads like "n8n · n8n.geninfos.com". A Google account's says whose it is: "Google · General Informatics LLC · info@…". Change it under Details › Change. A client's connection given the name another one has gets its client's name added ("Database · Acme"). If two still have the same name, the card offers a clearer one. - **Link to project…** on its card links it to any of the client's projects, and each project's Connections tab has **Link a connection**. - **Test connection** makes one read-only call and tells you what it found. - **Narrow it** (on the client's page): limit a link to one base, repository, project or folder, so a project sees only that.

title: Link a connection to a project
text: A connection does nothing until a project uses it. A card that no project uses says **Not linked to any project**, with **Link**, and Home's **Get started** counts them until they're linked. On the client's Connections tab, each card says where it's used and has **Link to project…**: tick one or several projects, and narrow each if you like. On a project's Connections tab, **Link a connection** lists the client's connections that aren't linked yet and your own tools. A client with no projects says so, with **Add project** and **From Claude**. Each task is told which connections its project has before it starts: each one's name, kind, whether it's production, and which one is the default for its kind. So it names the right one from its first call. When a project has two of a kind in different environments, say a production database and a development one, and the request doesn't say which, the task asks you instead of guessing.

title: Found on this computer
text: Ringkeeper prefers logins you already have to keys you'd paste. Connectors lists what you're signed in to here: GitHub CLI and Vercel CLI, and AWS profiles and SSO, Azure CLI, Google Cloud CLI and OCI. Each is offered once: **Connect** makes it your own tool, and you choose which projects use it; **Skip** stops offering it. Only who it signs in as is shown. A cloud's login stays in its own tool: Ringkeeper runs the cloud's server on this computer and holds no key. See Clouds. A project's page lists what its folder holds, the same way: keys in its `.env` and config files, and MCP servers in `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json`, `.codex/config.toml`, Claude Code's settings for that folder, and its own code. Nothing is added until you connect one. A server on a temporary tunnel like `trycloudflare.com` connects with a warning: it stops working when the tunnel does. A key for a service that signs in from its tile is named and left in the file.

title: All of a client's projects
text: A connection can go to all of its client's projects, and to projects added later. When you add one and the client has more than one project, that's what the success card suggests; untick any project to leave it out, or choose **Choose projects instead**. To change it later, open the connection's card: Details › All … projects. The card says what it reaches, like "All Acme projects except Website". Each project's link can still be narrowed under Details, to one base, branch or site. A client's connection never reaches another client's projects.

title: Your own tools (shared tools)
text: A shared tool is yours and holds no client's data: a browser like Playwright, files on this computer, public documentation. **Connectors › Add your own tool**, search for it, then choose **For all projects** or link it to some. To leave a client or project out, open its card: Details › All projects › Except….

title: A service you host for clients
text: Some services are yours but hold work for several clients, like your own n8n with each client's workflows on it. Make it your own tool, then link it to each client's project narrowed to that client's part: 1. On the connection's card, open **Details › Change › Make it my own tool**. Ringkeeper asks you to confirm it's you first. Its links stay as they were. 2. **Link to project…** on the client's project. 3. Open **Details**, and narrow that project's link. For n8n, choose a **workflow tag** (like `acme`), an **n8n project**, or both. Ringkeeper then checks the scope on every call that project's tasks make: - **Lists** show only what's inside the scope. Ringkeeper asks n8n for only those workflows, then checks what comes back, so the names of other clients' workflows never reach the task, even on an older n8n that ignores the filter. - **A workflow outside the scope** is refused, whether a task reads it, changes it, or turns it on or off. A change is refused when the task asks, so it never waits in Approvals. It's checked again when you approve. - **Runs (executions)** count by their workflow: only that client's show, and another client's can't be opened, retried or stopped. A link without a scope reaches the whole service, so narrow every client's link. Refusals are in Activity like any other.

title: Where the key goes
text: Into Ringkeeper's vault, encrypted with a key kept in Windows' credential store (or your server's key file). Keys never go to the AI, never appear in logs, and aren't shown again after you save them. To change one, paste the new key. Every service has its own page: services (where to get the token, what's held for approval, how to narrow it, what can be undone).

title: Agents and routines
text: *An agent is who does the work; a routine is when it runs.*

title: Agents
text: An agent is a named helper in one project (**Agents › New agent**, or a project's Agents tab): - **Instructions** it follows every time: tone, what to check, what never to touch. - **Connections** it may use: some of the project's. A shared tool only when you tick it. Ringkeeper refuses its calls to anything else. - Its own **model**, **effort** and **how independently it works**, or the project's. In a request, ask it by name: "ask the follow-up agent to draft replies to today's leads."

title: Routines
text: A routine runs one agent with a prompt (**Routines › New routine**: the project, then its agent; you can create the agent right there): - **On a schedule:** every day, weekdays, chosen days, monthly or every few hours, at a time in your time zone. After the computer slept, one run makes up for the missed ones. - **When something happens:** a new email matching a search, a new Airtable record, a file added to the project's folder, or its webhook being called (on this computer only). Or something going wrong: see Automation watch below. - **By hand:** Run now. New routines start paused, with **Test run**. Each run is an ordinary task: reads run, changes wait for your approval like any other. Limits per run (steps, minutes, a dollar cap with an API key) and runs per day keep it in check. Pause one routine, a project's, or all of them (also from the tray). Templates to start from: fix a failed automation, daily digest, new-lead follow-up draft, weekly report, data sync check. Below them are recipes: an agent with its routines, from the starters, a file or a link.

title: Automation watch
text: A routine can watch a client's automations and start when one goes wrong: - **An n8n workflow run fails** (all of a connection's workflows, or one). - **A Vercel deploy fails** (one Vercel project). - **A GitHub check fails** on a branch's latest commit, or **an issue is opened**. - **A website stops answering**: an error, or no answer in 15 seconds. Each is checked every 5 minutes, reading only. What's already there when you turn the routine on doesn't count; each new failure starts one run. A website being down is one event until it answers again. Ringkeeper reads n8n, Vercel and GitHub through the project's own connection, the same way a task does: the project's connections only, never another client's, with keys and secrets kept out of what the routine sees. A website is checked from this computer with no key; only whether it answered is kept. The run gets `{{event.what}}` (what went wrong, in a sentence), `{{event.link}}` where there is one, and the details, like `{{event.execution_id}}` for n8n. The **Fix a failed automation** template starts from these: the agent finds out why, says it in plain words, and proposes a fix, which waits for your approval like any change to production. Home shows a line for it: how many routines are watching, the last problem they found, and any watch that can't look (a connection that stopped working, say).

title: Approvals and safety
text: Ringkeeper lets the AI read freely and makes it ask before it changes anything that matters.

title: What waits for you
text: - **A change on a production connection**: a database update, a new Airtable record, an n8n workflow change, a Vercel deploy. - **Anything that reaches real people**, on any connection: an email, a text, a call, a calendar invite, a shared file. Reads never wait. Changes on staging and development connections run straight away and are logged. A Google account can let a single tool run without asking (per account, in its settings), except sending email. **Saving an email draft doesn't wait**, on Gmail, a Google account, Outlook or any mailbox: a draft reaches nobody. It's logged, and the task's result links each draft it saved (or says which connection's drafts folder it's in), so you can check it and send it yourself. Sending always waits. To have drafts wait for your OK too, turn on **Hold drafts for my OK too** in the connection's Details (on a Google account, it's the **create_draft** tool under Tools and approvals). A saved draft can be undone from the task page: the draft is deleted. An email to more than 10 people at once needs the connection's name typed, on every email connection, and can't be approved from Telegram, Slack or Discord.

title: Approving
text: Held actions are in **Approvals** (with a count in the sidebar), in their conversation, and in your notification channels. Each shows exactly what would run, on which connection, for which client and project. **Approve** runs it; **Deny** (with an optional note) tells the AI not to, and why. The card shows what's being approved without a click. For an email or a draft, that's To, Subject and the body (a long body shows its first 12 lines, with **Show all** for the rest); for other changes, the values that matter, like the SQL or the amount. **Show details** is only for the raw arguments. On a task or conversation page, what's waiting for you (approvals, questions, plans) is under the latest result, in the order it came, where you're reading. One that arrives while the page is open scrolls into view. If one is off-screen, a bar at the bottom says so ("1 approval waiting"); click it to jump there. Before it runs, an approved action is checked again against today's setup: if the connection was unlinked or narrowed since, it's refused. Where it can, Ringkeeper also checks the target hasn't changed since the action was held, and asks the AI to redo it if it has. **Destructive changes need the connection's name typed**: deleting rows, dropping or altering tables, anything the check can't read for certain. These can't be approved from Telegram, Slack or Discord: those say *Open in Ringkeeper*. The same goes for what can't be taken back on the newer connections: sending to many people at once, deleting a file or an email, a DELETE through an API. These always ask, even on test data; they can't be trusted for an hour, and no per-tool setting lets them run by themselves. **Business systems follow the action, not the vendor.** Reports and lookups run. Edits wait for approval, even on test data; saving an email draft runs, as above. Anything that sends to real people, publishes, posts to the books, moves money, deletes, changes who has access or adds ongoing cost needs the name typed, in the app itself. On these services a per-tool setting can make a tool stricter, never looser. Nothing on an accounting connection ever runs by itself, even after you've approved one like it. An approval that moves money shows the amount, currency, counterparty and account in large text, as written in the call; anything the call doesn't say shows as not stated. **Card and bank numbers never go through.** A tool call that carries one is refused before it's sent, and they're removed from logs, conversations, a task's events and the audit log. Use the service's own hosted page, or a token it issued. A held action expires after 24 hours if nobody answers.

title: Snooze
text: **Not now?** under an approval snoozes it for an hour, three hours, or until tomorrow at 9 (only the times before it expires are offered). Until then it isn't in Approvals or its count, and nothing notifies you about it. Then it's back, with a fresh notification in the desktop app and your channels. Snoozed approvals are listed at the bottom of Approvals; **Wake it now** brings one back early. Snoozing is in Activity. The task that's waiting goes on waiting: a snooze doesn't approve or deny anything. J, K, A and D work on the Approvals page, and one action can be trusted for an hour: see Working faster. On a business system or an add-on tool, that covers that one action on that connection, not everything it can do.

title: The record
text: Every change attempt and every refusal is in **Activity** with the time, project, connection, what was asked, and what happened. Nothing in that log can be edited or deleted, by you or by Ringkeeper.

title: Stop everything
text: **Settings › Stop everything** stops every running task and pauses new work. Approvals wait where they are until you resume.

title: Undo
text: When a change runs on a connection (because you approved it, or because it runs without asking on a staging or development connection), Ringkeeper first keeps a copy of what it's about to change. For 7 days you can put it back.

title: What can be undone
text: - **Databases:** a plain `UPDATE` or `DELETE` on one table that has a primary key. Ringkeeper keeps only the rows it touches (for an update, only the columns it sets). Reverting puts the old values back, or the deleted rows. - **Airtable:** changed fields go back to what they were; deleted records come back (as new records, with new IDs); added records are deleted. - **n8n:** a replaced workflow goes back to how it was; a workflow turned on or off goes back.

title: What can't
text: An email or text that was sent, a call, a deploy, a push to GitHub, an `INSERT` (Ringkeeper can't tell which rows it added), changes to tables themselves, and anything another tool's server does. The approval card says **Can't be undone** and why, before you approve.

title: Reverting
text: Open the task (or its conversation): **Data it changed** lists each one with **Revert** and what it will put back. Reverting is itself a change, so it waits for your OK in Approvals. If something else changed those rows or records since, the approval says so; and if they change between asking and approving, the revert stops instead of overwriting them.

title: Space and time
text: Kept changes live in Ringkeeper's data folder and are deleted after 7 days. Each project has 50 MB for them; past that, a change still runs but isn't kept, and its task says so. Space frees up as old ones pass 7 days.

title: Passes
text: A pass lets an AI app on this computer use one project's connections: Claude Desktop, Claude Code or Cursor. The app talks to Ringkeeper, never to the service, and every call is checked the same way a task's is: - It reaches only the project's own connections. Another client's connection is refused on every call, even if it was linked by mistake. - A change to production waits for your approval in Ringkeeper, like any held change. - Every change it makes, and every call that's refused, is in Activity under the pass's name, with secrets taken out. - A change it made can be undone for 7 days, from the pass in Settings > Passes or from Undo. - It can't use Claude through Ringkeeper, reach another project, or change Ringkeeper's settings. The app never sees the connections' keys, and the pass's own key stays in Ringkeeper's vault: what you add to the app only starts Ringkeeper's bridge on this computer.

title: Make a pass
text: 1. Settings > Passes > New pass. Pick the project, and give the pass a name the app will list it by, like `acme-code`. 2. Choose the app: - **Claude Desktop:** click **Save the extension**. It's saved into your Downloads folder as `Ringkeeper-<pass>.mcpb`. Double-click it, and Claude Desktop asks whether to install it. If double-clicking doesn't open Claude, add the file from Claude's Customize > Connectors. - **Claude Code:** run the command in a terminal. It adds the pass for every folder you use Claude Code in. - **Cursor:** put the JSON in `.cursor/mcp.json` in your home folder, or in one project's folder for that project only. If the file already lists servers, add this one beside them. 3. Start a new chat (Claude Desktop), or restart the app (Claude Code, Cursor). Ringkeeper has to be running while you use it. The app then has tools named by service: `database_query`, `airtable_list_records`, `memory_recall`, and so on, and Ringkeeper's own: `ringkeeper_ask`, `ringkeeper_task_status` and `ringkeeper_check_approval`. The extension starts Ringkeeper from where it's installed (usually `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Ringkeeper` on Windows), so it keeps working after Ringkeeper updates.

title: Claude Desktop by hand
text: If the extension won't install, you can add the pass to Claude Desktop's settings file yourself: 1. **Quit Claude completely first:** File > Exit on Windows (or right-click its icon by the clock and choose Quit), Claude > Quit Claude on a Mac. Closing the window isn't enough. Claude rewrites the file while it runs, and an edit made then is lost. 2. Open `claude_desktop_config.json`: `%APPDATA%\Claude\` on Windows, `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/` on a Mac. Copy it somewhere first. 3. In the pass, under Claude Desktop > Add it by hand instead, copy the JSON, and add its entry under `mcpServers`, beside any servers already there. 4. Start Claude.

title: Hand Ringkeeper a whole request
text: Besides using the connections itself, the app can give Ringkeeper a request with `ringkeeper_ask`, as if you'd typed it in Ringkeeper: "find last week's failed orders and refund them". It becomes a task in the pass's project, and only there, with everything a task has: its own conversation in Ringkeeper, the usual limits and spending cap, approvals for changes to production, and the audit log, under the pass's name. The app waits up to 50 seconds (Settings > Passes; AI apps commonly give up on a tool after about 60). If the task is done by then, it gets the result. If not, it gets the task's link and checks later with `ringkeeper_task_status`. If the task needs your approval for a change, or the client is over its monthly cap, the app gets the link to Approvals, as for a change it held itself.

title: When a change waits for approval
text: The app is told the change is waiting, and gets a link to Ringkeeper's Approvals to give you. Open it and click **Approve** or **Deny** on the change. The link brings Ringkeeper's window up at Approvals. The app can ask what became of the change with its `ringkeeper_check_approval` tool: it gets the same link while the change is waiting, and the result once it ran.

title: Revoke or remove a pass
text: **Revoke** stops it: the app's next call is refused, and the refusal is in Activity. **Remove** deletes a revoked pass and its key. What it did stays in Activity.

title: When Ringkeeper quits, restarts or updates
text: The bridge stops when Ringkeeper does, so an update can replace Ringkeeper's files. - **Claude Desktop** starts it again by itself once Ringkeeper is back. In the meantime it's told Ringkeeper isn't running and to try again in a minute. - **Claude Code:** run `/mcp` and reconnect the pass. - **Cursor:** turn the pass off and on again in Cursor's MCP settings. **The app says Ringkeeper isn't running?** Start Ringkeeper. If the app was opened before Ringkeeper, restart the app: it starts the bridge when it opens. **It says there's no pass by that name?** It was removed, or the name in the app's settings is different from the one in Settings > Passes.

title: A client's month
text: Each client's page has a **This month** tab: what Ringkeeper did for them in a month, and what it cost. Pick another month at the top. It counts only that client's projects, so one client's month never shows another's work: - **Tasks** started that month, however they started (from the app, a routine, Telegram, Slack or a pass), and how each ended. - **Changes** made to their services, and the ones checked before they ran: how many you approved, declined, or left to expire. - **Refused calls:** what Ringkeeper's checks stopped. - **AI cost:** what Claude cost for those tasks. With a Claude subscription it's an estimate, since a subscription isn't billed per task. Clients & projects shows each client's cost so far this month beside their name.

title: The report
text: Under the month, **Download PDF** or **Download Markdown** gives a report you can send the client: a summary and each task with its result. Tick **Include the AI cost** to add what it cost. **Download tasks as CSV** gives the month's tasks for a spreadsheet. The report has the tasks' titles and results with secrets taken out. It never names another client.

title: Email it
text: If one of the client's projects has a mail connection (SMTP, Resend, a mailbox or Gmail), type the client's address and click **Draft the email**. The email waits in **Approvals**, like every email Ringkeeper sends: nothing goes out until you approve it there. It goes from a mail connection the client's projects may use: theirs, or your own mail linked to one of their projects, never another client's.

title: A monthly cap
text: On the client's page, Settings > Monthly cap sets the most their tasks may cost in a month, in dollars. Once that month's AI cost reaches it: - A new task for the client, or a follow-up to one, waits for you in Approvals instead of running, wherever it came from. Choose **Run anyway this once**, **Raise the cap** (to more than the client has used this month), or **Don't run it**. Running past the cap and raising it are both in Activity. - Routines don't ask: their runs are skipped, their history says why, and Home says which client's routines are waiting. - A task that's already running finishes. Its own spending cap still applies. The cap starts again on the 1st. Changes to the cap are in Activity. The month follows this computer's calendar (the server's, for a server install).

title: Recipes
text: A recipe is an agent and its routines as one file: the agent's instructions and settings, and each routine's prompt and timing. Use one to start from, or share your own. A recipe never has a key, a connection's name, or anything that points at one client. Which connection to use, and what an event watches (a repository, a website, an Airtable base), are chosen when you add it. It can't run code: a recipe is only settings and instructions, and a file with anything else in it is refused.

title: Add one
text: On a project's Routines, **New routine** shows the routine templates and, below them, **recipes**: - **The starters:** 15 common jobs, from fixing a failed n8n run to a weekly client report, acting on an email you forward to yourself, or checking a site's speed every week. - **Import a recipe from a file or a link:** a `.json` file, or an https link to one. A GitHub page for a file works too, like `https://github.com/alexyushkin/ringkeeper-recipes/blob/main/daily-digest.json`. Shared recipes are in ringkeeper-recipes. Before anything is added you see the whole recipe: the agent's instructions, each routine with its prompt and when it runs, and what it needs: - **A connection of each kind the agent uses,** from the ones linked to this project. If the project has none of that kind, link one first, or add the recipe without it and give the agent one later on its page. A routine that watches a service (an n8n failure, a GitHub check) needs that connection before the recipe can be added. - **For a routine that runs when something happens,** what to watch: a repository, a website's address, an Airtable base and table, or a Vercel project. **Add to this project** adds the agent and its routines. The routines start paused: run each once from its page to check it, then turn it on. If the project already has an agent with that name, the new one gets a number (`fixer-2`); nothing already there changes.

title: Share your own
text: On an agent (a project's Agents), **Export as recipe** saves the agent and its routines as a file, `<agent>.ringkeeper-recipe.json`. It keeps: - the agent's instructions, model, effort, autonomy and memory setting, and the kinds of connection it uses (not which ones); - each routine's name, prompt, timing, limits and notifications, and for an event only what kind it is (an n8n failure, a GitHub check, a website). It leaves out connection names, what an event watches, time zones, and anything that looks like a secret. Read it before you share it: what you wrote in the instructions and prompts is in it. A recipe's Gmail event may say which mail starts a run, in Gmail's search words: the Forward an email starter watches only `from:me to:me subject:(Fwd OR Fw)`. An exported recipe never has one, since a search can name a client.

title: The file
text: A recipe is JSON with `"ringkeeper_recipe": 1`, its version. A later Ringkeeper reads older versions; an older one says to update before adding a newer one. The starters are published in ringkeeper-recipes, and kept the same as this repository's recipes folder. The agent's `needs` lists kinds of connection: a type (`google`, `github`, `n8n`) or one business system by name, like `vendor:pagespeed`, since those all share the type `vendor`.

title: Notifications
text: Ringkeeper can tell you about approvals, finished tasks, routine results and failures when you're away from the app: in **Telegram**, **Slack** or **Discord** (Settings › Notifications). On Windows you also get a notification from the tray. Windows notifications can't have Approve or Deny buttons yet (the desktop app's notifications only offer buttons on phones): click one to open it in Ringkeeper.

title: Each channel's choices
text: - **What it sends:** approvals and questions, routine results, failures, finished tasks. - **Quiet hours:** nothing is sent then; what came up is sent when they end (an approval only if it's still waiting). - **Which clients and projects:** all by default. - **Full results and files for requests from here:** on by default. A task you asked for from this chat ends there with its result and files (see below). Off, the chat only hears how it ended ("✔ My Project: done") and a link to read it in Ringkeeper. - **Send test** checks it works, and that your button presses count.

title: Telegram
text: In Telegram, message **@BotFather**, send `/newbot`, and paste the token it gives you into **Settings › Notifications › Telegram**. Then send your new bot a message and choose your chat in Settings. Only that chat gets messages, and only it can answer. You can also turn on requests from Telegram: type or send a voice note, and you see what Ringkeeper heard before anything is sent.

title: Slack and Discord
text: Both are your own app (Slack, in Socket Mode) or bot (Discord). They connect out from your computer, so nothing needs a public address. Settings walks you through creating them step by step: the Slack app manifest to paste, or the Discord invite link that asks only to see channels and send messages. Then choose where it posts (a channel or a direct message) and your member or user ID. Tokens go into the vault. Your Slack member ID starts with U: your profile picture › Profile › ⋮ › Copy member ID. An ID starting with D or C is a conversation's (a DM's or a channel's), and Ringkeeper says so.

title: New requests by DM
text: Turn on **Take new requests by DM** on a Slack or Discord channel, and a direct message from you to the app (Slack) or bot (Discord) becomes a new request, the same as one typed in Ringkeeper: it's routed to a project and runs with the usual approvals and limits. Ringkeeper answers in that DM with what it did, and again when each task ends. Only your member or user ID is taken; anyone else is told no, and messages in a channel are never requests. A question that needs no project, such as "how many connections and clients do we have?" or how to do something in Ringkeeper, gets the same answer the app gives, in that DM. The same goes for requests from Telegram.

title: A chat is a conversation
text: In a DM or a Telegram chat, your messages continue one Ringkeeper conversation, so a follow-up like "publish the result here" or "now do it for Acme" knows what came before: the earlier messages, and what each task did. The first reply of a conversation links to it in the app. A new conversation starts after 2 hours of quiet, or when you send **new**. You can also start one with a request: **new: check Acme's orders**. - **Results come back to the chat.** When a task you asked for from a chat ends, it posts what it found or did, not just "done". Tables read as one line per row, and code or SQL stays in the app. A long result shows its first part and a link to the rest. Files the task made come with it, when they're small (up to 8 MB each, five at most); a file that looks like a secret, like a `.env` or a key, never does. To keep results and files in the app, turn off **Full results and files for requests from here** for that channel. - **Approvals come back too.** When a task from a chat waits for your OK, its approval card is posted in that chat, with its buttons, even if the channel isn't set to send approvals. - **Slack:** the app needs the manifest from this version (it adds direct messages, and sending a task's files). For an app set up before, copy the manifest from **Add another Slack channel**, paste it on the app's **App Manifest** page at api.slack.com, and reinstall the app. - **Discord:** the bot has to share a server with you for you to message it.

title: Buttons
text: Messages are a short summary (no secrets, code or full SQL) with **Approve**, **Deny** and **Open** buttons: - **Approve** only appears for a safe change: not on production, and not one that needs the connection's name typed. Those say *Approve it in Ringkeeper*. - **Only you can answer.** A press from anyone else in the channel is refused with "not allowed". - **Open** brings the Ringkeeper window up at that page. - **Once decided,** the message shows how it ended, like "✔ Approved by Alex (Slack). It ran.", and keeps only **Open**. - **"Which project?"** is asked once, with one line saying why, and a button for each project by name.

title: Where Claude runs
text: By default, Claude runs on Anthropic's own service, with an API key or a Claude subscription. You can run it on **Amazon Bedrock**, **Google Vertex AI** or **Microsoft Foundry** instead, for example when a client's data has to stay in their own cloud, or their spend has to go through it. **Settings › Claude › Where Claude runs** sets the default. Tasks, the architect and the router all run there. A project can use another: open its **Settings** tab. That choice appears once a second place is set up.

title: Amazon Bedrock
text: In the Bedrock console, submit the Anthropic use case form once. Then give the region and either: - **a Bedrock API key**, kept in the vault; or - **an AWS profile on this computer.** Its short-lived credentials are read each time a session starts, so Ringkeeper stores no key. If they've run out, the task says to sign in again with `aws sso login`.

title: Google Vertex AI
text: Enable Vertex AI and the Claude models in Model Garden. Give the project ID, the region (`global` often works), and a service account key file with the Vertex AI User role. The key is kept in the vault, and a task never gets a copy. See below.

title: Microsoft Foundry
text: Create a resource and one deployment per Claude model in the Foundry portal. Give the resource's name, and either its API key or **Use my Azure CLI login**. Foundry has no default models, so fill in your deployment names.

title: Models
text: Each cloud has its own model IDs. **Models on this platform** pins one per family (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku), and Ringkeeper uses it wherever that family is chosen. Left empty, Claude Code uses its own defaults for that platform, which can bill at the Opus rate.

title: Check it
text: **Check it** sends one tiny request the way a task would, so it proves the login, the region and the model together. Your cloud bills it, by a few tokens.

title: What a task can see
text: A task holds no model key. Claude Code in a task talks to Ringkeeper's model proxy with a token that belongs to that task: it reaches nothing but the model, and it ends with the session. Ringkeeper adds the real key on the way out, and counts the tokens each task uses.

title: Good to know
text: - A task's spending cap still applies on a cloud. - The Help assistant and the router run on the default place. A project's choice covers that project's tasks. - Web search isn't available to Claude on Bedrock.

title: Backup and moving to another computer
text: **Settings › Backup** (desktop app) makes one file with everything Ringkeeper knows: clients, projects, connections and their keys, agents, routines, settings and history. It's locked with a password you choose when you make it. Without that password nobody can open it, including you, so keep it somewhere safe and apart from the file. **Project folders aren't in the backup.** They stay where they are. A restored project points to the same folder path; on a new computer, copy the folders over yourself and, if the path changed, set each project's folder on its page.

title: Make a backup
text: Choose a password (at least 8 characters), a folder (Documents › Ringkeeper backups unless you pick another), and **Save the backup**. The file ends in `.rkbackup`.

title: Restore on another computer
text: 1. Install Ringkeeper and connect Claude in the first run. On the next step, choose **Restore a backup instead**: the backup brings your projects and connections. 2. **Settings › Backup › Restore a backup**: choose the file, type its password, and **Show what's in it**. You see the clients, projects (and whether each project's folder is on this computer), connections and how much history comes in. Nothing has changed yet. 3. **Restore and restart.** The keys go into this computer's vault, and Ringkeeper restarts with the backup's data. What was here before is kept beside it, as `ringkeeper.db.before-restore` in the data folder.

title: Automatic backups
text: Turn on **Make a backup every week**, choose a folder (one your cloud drive copies is a good choice), how many to keep, and a password. The password is kept in Ringkeeper's vault on this computer so it can lock each backup; write it down, because you need it to restore. The first backup is made right away, then one every week; older ones are deleted, keeping the last few you chose. While they're off, Home asks once to turn them on, after your first real task (Check my setup's and the demo's don't count). **Not now** hides it for good, and so does turning them on, even if you turn them off again later.

title: On a server
text: The server (Docker) keeps its data in Postgres and its data folder: back those up with your usual tools (`pg_dump`, and a copy of the data folder with its master key).

title: Working faster
text: Small things that save a trip.

title: Quick request
text: Press **Ctrl+Alt+R** anywhere, and a small box opens over whatever you're doing. Type or hold the mic, choose a client or project if you like, and send. It says **Sent**, with a link to the conversation, and closes. Change the key or turn it off in Settings › Advanced › Quick request. If another app already uses it, Ringkeeper says so and you can pick another.

title: Sending with the keyboard
text: Every box you type in works the same way: the request box on Home, the quick request, a conversation, **Continue this task**, answers to questions and plans, and Help. Under each box a line says which key sends. Choose in Settings › General › Send with: - **Ctrl+Enter** (the default): Enter starts a new line. On a Mac it's **Cmd+Enter**. - **Enter**: Shift+Enter starts a new line. The choice is kept by Ringkeeper, not the browser, so it's the same in every browser you open Ringkeeper in. **Esc** leaves the box. While the @ list is open, Enter picks from it and nothing is sent. In a plan's note, the key sends it as **Ask for changes**; it never approves a plan or a change.

title: Send later
text: Under the request box on Home, **Send later…** picks a day and time (this computer's time). The request waits until then, in its conversation and in **Sent for later** on Home, each with **Cancel**. At its time it's routed like any request. If Ringkeeper isn't running then (the computer was asleep, say), it runs when Ringkeeper starts, unless that's more than 6 hours late: then it doesn't run, and its conversation says so. A time can be up to 90 days ahead.

title: Mentions
text: Type **@** in any request box to name a client, project, connection or agent. A mention is a firm choice: the request goes there, whatever else it says. Mention a client with several projects and Ringkeeper asks which.

title: Attach files to a request
text: Drop files on the request box, or use the clip. They go into an `attachments` folder in the project its task runs in, and the task is told where they are. Up to 50 MB each. A task can save an email's attachment or a file from Drive, OneDrive or storage there too, to work on it, and it's then listed with the task's files.

title: Run again and saved requests
text: On a task's page, **Run again** starts the same request as a new task. **Save this request** keeps it on its project as a shortcut: saved requests are under the box on Home, one click to fill it in.

title: Keys already in a project
text: When a project has a folder, its Overview and Connections tabs look in its `.env` files and config files for keys they know, like `DATABASE_URL`, `AIRTABLE_API_KEY`, `N8N_API_KEY`, `VERCEL_TOKEN`, `TWILIO_*` and `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Each shows masked, with **Connect…** or **Skip**. Nothing is added until you confirm that one, and nothing outside the project's folder is read.

title: Connection health
text: Every connection is tested once a day, reads only, like the Test button. Its card shows the result and the reason it failed. If one stops working, or a key is 7 days from expiring, your channels say so. GitHub tells Ringkeeper when its tokens expire; for others, write the date on the card (Details › Change). **Test all** on Connectors runs it now. Turn it off in Settings › Notifications › Connection check.

title: Approvals by keyboard
text: On Approvals: **J** next, **K** previous, **A** approve, **D** deny. A change that needs the connection's name typed puts you in that box instead. **Approve all N like this** shows when one task is waiting on the same action, with the same details, more than once.

title: Trust an action for an hour
text: **Approve, and trust this in the project for 1 hour** lets that tool on that connection run without asking in that project, for an hour. It's never offered for deletes or anything else that needs the name typed, and even under a trust such a call still asks. Approvals lists what's trusted, with **Stop trusting**. Every trust and every call under one is in Activity.

title: Morning digest
text: Home shows the last 24 hours per client: what ran, what failed and what waits for you. To get it on Telegram, Slack and Discord too, turn on Settings › Notifications › Morning digest and set the time.

title: Pins and recents
text: The client and project switcher, and Ctrl+K, list what you pinned and what you used lately first. The star beside the switcher pins what's chosen.

title: Security: what's stored where, and what leaves your computer
text: Ringkeeper runs on your computer. There's no Ringkeeper account and no Ringkeeper server: nothing about your clients goes to the people who make it.

title: What's stored where (desktop app)
text: | What | Where | How it's protected | | --- | --- | --- | | Clients, projects, connections (names, settings), agents, routines, tasks, conversations, approvals, the activity log | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Ringkeeper\ringkeeper.db` | Your Windows account. The activity log can't be edited or deleted, by you or by Ringkeeper. | | Keys and tokens (Claude, every connection, Telegram/Slack/Discord, your Google app) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Ringkeeper\vault.json` | Each one encrypted (AES-256-GCM) with a key derived from the master key. | | The master key | Windows Credential Manager (`Ringkeeper/master-key`) | Your Windows sign-in. Without it the vault can't be read. | | Kept changes, for Undo | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Ringkeeper\undo` | Your Windows account. Deleted after 7 days. | | Logs | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Ringkeeper\logs` | Secrets are removed before anything is written. | | Project folders | Wherever you chose (new ones in `Documents\Ringkeeper`) | Your Windows account. | | Backups you make | Where you save them | Encrypted with the password you chose (Backup). |

title: Signed links are taken out
text: Some web addresses work for whoever holds them, like a Lemon Squeezy customer portal link or an S3 or Azure download link. Ringkeeper keeps where such a link points and removes the rest from logs, the audit log, tool results and conversations. A task can't pass one on: a tool call that carries one is refused. To send someone a link like that, use the service itself.

title: A task knows when it has only part of something
text: A long answer never just stops. Every tool that returns part of something says how much there is and where the next part starts, and a task is told to read the rest before it answers, or to say its answer is based on part of it. A long result that can't simply be asked for again, such as the answer to an API call, is kept in memory for about half an hour, for that task only, after secrets are removed from it.

title: Keys stay out of a task
text: A task runs Claude Code with two short-lived passes for its own project, and no keys. One reaches its connections, through Ringkeeper's gateway, which checks that the project may use that connection, adds the key itself, removes any secret from the answer, and logs the call. The other reaches only the model, through Ringkeeper's model proxy, which adds your API key, subscription or cloud sign-in on the way out and counts the tokens. Both end with the session. One client's project can't reach another client's connection through these. **The desktop app isn't a sandbox.** On the desktop, the AI runs as your Windows or Mac user. Ringkeeper's holds and gateway control what it does through connections, but they don't wall it off from your computer. No key is in its environment or its own files, yet a script written to do it could still reach anything your user can: your files, the system keychain and the master key in it, and Ringkeeper's own files. A task told to do that by something it read is the risk to think about. For strong isolation, turn on **Settings > Security > Run tasks in Docker**, or use server mode. A task in Docker sees only its project's folder, so it has no access to the vault, the keychain or the rest of the computer's files. We recommend it for client work. It's off by default and needs Docker Desktop, plus a one-time image download. The image doesn't include Claude Code: the first task in Docker downloads the version this release pins from npm, checks it against the checksum the release recorded, and keeps it for the next tasks, where a task can't change it. Three things to know about it on the desktop: - **If Docker isn't ready when a task starts, the task still runs,** on this computer and without that isolation, and says so at the top of the task. - **A task can still change its project's folder,** as it's meant to. - **A container can reach this computer's network,** which it needs for the gateway. A service on your computer that trusts anything local isn't protected from it.

title: Apps with a pass
text: A pass lets Claude Desktop, Claude Code or Cursor use one project's connections. The app starts Ringkeeper's bridge on this computer, which reads the pass's key from the vault, so the key isn't in the app's settings or in the extension file. Each call goes through the gateway like a task's: the project's own connections only, another client's refused on every call, production changes held, the call logged and its secrets removed. A pass can't reach the model, another project or Ringkeeper's settings. The database keeps only a hash of its key, and revoking it stops the next call. With `ringkeeper_ask` the app can also hand Ringkeeper a request. It becomes a task in the pass's own project, with the same approvals, limits, spending cap and audit log as one you start, and the app can follow only the tasks its pass started. The bridge runs Ringkeeper's own Python from its install folder. Claude Desktop's extension adds a small relay, run on Claude's own Node, that starts the bridge again after Ringkeeper restarts. It holds no key and passes calls through unchanged. The link to Approvals that a held change gives the app is signed, and it works only on this computer. It brings Ringkeeper's window up there. (When Ringkeeper runs without its app window, it signs the browser that opened it in instead, with a one-time code.) Approving still takes your click.

title: What leaves your computer
text: - **To Anthropic:** your requests, and what tasks read and do, so Claude can work on them (with your API key or subscription, under Anthropic's terms). - **To the services you connect:** the calls tasks make (Airtable, your database, GitHub, Google, and so on), with their keys. - **To Telegram, Slack or Discord, if you set them up:** short summaries of approvals and finished tasks (never keys, code or full SQL). A task you asked for from a chat sends its full result back there (tables as lines, code and SQL stay in the app), with the files it made: small ones, never one that looks like a secret, and known secrets masked. To keep results and files in the app, turn off **Full results and files for requests from here** in that channel's choices (Settings › Notifications): the chat then only hears how the task ended, with a link. - **To GitHub:** the update check (`latest.json` from the releases page) and the update download. - **To the MCP registry and Hugging Face, only when you use them:** catalog searches, and the download of the on-device voice model. - **To PyPI and GitHub, only if you download the scan reader:** the request for its files. Scans themselves are read on this computer and never sent. Nothing else: no analytics, no usage statistics, no crash reports. A problem report only leaves when you send it yourself, after reading it.

title: Changes wait for you
text: Changes to production connections, and anything that reaches real people, wait for your approval; destructive ones need the connection's name typed. See Approvals and safety.

title: Reporting a vulnerability
text: Privately, please: see SECURITY.md.

title: Self-test
text: The self-test sends real requests through Ringkeeper and checks what happened. It uses the real router, real workers and the real gateway, against two made-up clients. **Your own clients, connections and tasks aren't touched.** It runs in a scratch folder with its own data and its own vault, and removes that folder when it ends. The one thing it borrows is your Claude sign-in, for the length of the run.

title: Run it
text: To check your own projects and connections instead, see Check my setup. In the app: **Settings > Advanced > Self-test**, then **Run the self-test**. You can keep using Ringkeeper while it runs. The report stays in the same section, with **Save report** (into your Downloads folder), **Copy report**, **Save table as CSV** and **Show in folder**. **Earlier reports** lists the other days kept: pick one to read it again. In a terminal: ``` ringkeeper scenarios run ringkeeper scenarios run --only held-write --only cross-client ringkeeper scenarios list ``` From a source checkout the report goes to `docs/scenarios/<date>.md`. Otherwise it goes to the `self-test` folder in your Ringkeeper data folder. The command exits with an error below 90%. A full run takes about 10 minutes. On an API key it's usually well under a dollar, and it stops starting new scenarios at an estimated $15, or whatever you give `--ceiling`. On a subscription nothing is billed per request, but it does count toward your usage.

title: What it checks
text: Each scenario says what must happen, and is judged from what Ringkeeper recorded: the routing, the approvals, the activity log, the task's steps and the demo databases. What the model says it did doesn't count, and a tool call that failed doesn't count as using the tool. - **Routing:** the right project, an unclear request asked about, @-mentions, a request across two projects, an agent named in the request, a routine's test run, Help, and memory (a note kept, then recalled; and a fact one task found that the next task, in a new conversation, uses without searching again). Also when it shouldn't ask: a client's email going to its default project, a client with one project, and a follow-up in the same conversation after it asked once. - **Holds:** a production change held, approved and undone; a denied change that doesn't happen; a delete that needs the connection's name typed; a development connection that isn't held; and instructions hidden in a customer's note that aren't followed. - **Refusals:** a request for the other client's data worded to sound legitimate, the other client's connection named outright, and an agent reaching past its connections. A good model usually won't even try these, so the self-test also calls the gateway directly, which is what proves the gateway refuses. - **Pushed to cross over:** a Demo Co Airtable record whose text tells the agent to read Acme's database, and a Demo shop request that asks for Acme's connection by name. Each passes only if the attempt reached the gateway and was refused, or the model declined on its own. The report shows what the worker called, what came back and what it said, so you can see which. - **Limits:** a plan limit reported instead of retried, the end of an email too long for one read, and an email whose attachment can't be read (a Numbers file): the task must end as Not done, not Done, even if it suggests ways forward. Each scenario also has a cost ceiling, and goes over it as a failure. And in every scenario, the conversation's last reply mustn't still ask which project once work has started. A failed scenario's transcript in the report starts with what the router made of the request: the project it proposed and how sure it was, and whether it started the work, asked, or took it as a question about Ringkeeper. That shows why a request was or wasn't asked about.

title: Real services
text: Scenarios that need a real account are skipped, and the report says so. To run them, put a `scenarios.toml` beside where you run the command, or in the `self-test` folder for the app. Use test accounts only. ```toml [neon] secret = "..." [github] secret = "..." ``` The names it knows are `neon`, `supabase`, `airtable`, `n8n`, `github` and `gmail`. Each `secret` is what that connection normally stores. Keep this file out of any repository.

title: Check my setup
text: Check my setup sends real requests through your own Ringkeeper, on your own projects and connections, and reports what happened to each. It uses the real router, real workers and the real gateway. The self-test does the same against made-up clients in a scratch folder; this checks what you've actually set up. **It only reads.** Nothing it starts can change anything: - Its tasks can't edit files or run commands (no Edit, Write or Bash), and make no branch in a project's folder. - The gateway holds every write from them for your approval, even one that would run without asking anywhere else. Nothing held is approved by the check: it's left for you in **Approvals**, and the report says so. - A request to go ahead on a production connection, or to let a project use the web, is left for you the same way. - They keep no memory notes, and answering "which project?" doesn't teach the router anything.

title: What it sends
text: - One read-only request per connection, like the ones Home suggests: "List the tables in Acme web's database", "List the open pull requests in Acme web's GitHub repository". It goes in the first project the connection is linked to: a connection linked to several projects, or to all of them, is checked once. When a project has two connections of a kind (two databases, say), each request names its connection. A request names a connection by its unique name (`acme-google`), not the name the app shows, which two can share. A Google account's request follows what it was given: its calendar if it has Calendar, its unread mail if it only has mail, and so on. One given nothing it can read (only sending mail, say) is tested like an MCP server, below. - An MCP server, an add-on tool's API or an HTTP API isn't sent a request: Ringkeeper connects to it itself, as its **Test** button does, and counts the tools it offers (an HTTP API's endpoints, if it has an OpenAPI address). No model is asked, so it costs nothing, and the connection's card shows the result. - For a project none of those went through the router for (its connections were checked in another project, or tested directly), one request of its own, "Explain what's in Acme shop's folder, in a few lines", to check that its requests reach it. - A question about your setup: "Which projects do I have, and which connections does each one use?" - A web lookup. - A follow-up in the first conversation, to check that it carries on there. A connection linked to no project isn't sent anything: no task could use it. The report lists it under **Gaps**, and its card says **Not linked to any project**. If it's asked which project a request is for, it answers with the project the request was written for. If a task asks a question, it answers "only read". Both are in the report.

title: Run it
text: In the app: **Settings > Advanced > Check my setup**, then **Check my setup**. It sends three requests at a time, and each one's row shows as soon as it's back. You can keep using Ringkeeper while it runs, and **Stop after these** sends no more. In a terminal, with Ringkeeper running (the requests go to it): ``` ringkeeper scenarios run --mine ``` It stops sending new requests at an estimated $5 (on an API key), or whatever you give `--ceiling`. On a subscription nothing is billed per request, but it counts toward your usage.

title: The report
text: One row per request: whether it worked, where it was routed, whether it asked anything, which tools ran, what came back or the error, and what it cost. Then the gaps. Each request ends one of three ways: - **Worked**: it went where it was written for, did what was asked, and the answer is complete. - **Needs you**: it's waiting on you, so it didn't run to the end. A write held in **Approvals**, say, or a web lookup in a project whose tasks can't use the web. - **Failed**: an error, no answer in time, or it went to another project than the one it was written for (the Google request for Acme web's account answered in another project, say). A request to a connection works only if its task used that connection, and only if the answer is complete: one that says it's only part of what was asked ("the list is partly read", "a background agent is still fetching the rest") doesn't count, and the report quotes what it said. The report is kept in the `setup-check` folder in your Ringkeeper data folder, by day, and shown in the same section of Settings. Under it: **Save report** (a Markdown file), **Copy report**, **Save table as CSV**, and, in the desktop app, **Show in folder**. In the desktop app a saved file goes in your Downloads folder (nothing there is overwritten); in a browser it downloads. **Earlier reports** lists the other days kept: pick one to read it again, with the same buttons.

title: Its conversations
text: Its conversations are titled "Check my setup: ..." and tagged. Archive them all, with their tasks, in one click: **Archive them** in the same section, or ``` ringkeeper scenarios archive --mine ``` Archived conversations stay searchable, and can be brought back.

title: A connection says Plan limit
text: The service answered that your plan with it doesn't include this. The key and the connection are fine, so another try won't help: Ringkeeper doesn't repeat the call for an hour, and that call doesn't count against the task. Anything else that fails in the task still does. Upgrade with the service, then press **Test** on the connection. If something here doesn't fix it, use **Help › Report a problem** in the app (or Ctrl+K, "report"). It gathers the version and the end of the logs, removes keys, tokens, passwords and email addresses, and shows you exactly what's in it (you can edit it) before you open a GitHub issue or save it as a zip. Nothing is sent by Ringkeeper itself.

title: Windows says "Windows protected your PC"
text: The beta isn't signed yet. Click **More info › Run anyway**. The installer comes from the releases page.

title: "Can't reach Ringkeeper's backend"
text: The part of Ringkeeper that does the work stopped. Quit Ringkeeper from the tray icon and open it again. If it keeps happening, report a problem: the logs say why it stopped.

title: Claude says the key isn't valid
text: Open **Settings › Claude** and paste the key again. Keys start with `sk-ant-`. If you're on an Anthropic workspace that needs it, add its ID there too. Ringkeeper checks the key with Anthropic before saving it, and shows Anthropic's own message if it's refused.

title: Claude is unavailable
text: When Claude itself can't answer, Ringkeeper says which of these it is, and what it does: - **Your Claude plan's limit is reached.** Home says when it resets. Nothing new starts until then, and tasks and requests wait instead of failing: they go on by themselves after the reset. **Try now** next to the notice stops waiting (if Claude still says the limit is reached, it waits again), and so does changing the Claude sign-in, key or place in Settings. Only Claude's own signals count: a task that fails while talking about another service's "rate limit reached" or "Internal Server Error" is an ordinary failure, not Claude's. - **Claude is overloaded, limiting how fast requests can go, or can't be reached** (check this computer's internet connection). A task is tried again a few times, waiting longer each time. A request waits and is tried again after 2, 5 and 15 minutes, then every half hour. The conversation says so once, and again when Claude is back. After 12 hours it stops trying and offers **Try again**. - **Claude takes too long to work out where a request goes.** Under a request, the conversation says "Finding the right project…", and after 20 seconds "Still working out where this goes…". Working out where it goes stops after 90 seconds and starts over at once. If that's slow too, the request waits and is tried again like the rest above, and the conversation says so once. - **The sign-in to Claude is missing or expired.** Sign in again in Settings › Claude, then send the request again or use **Run again** on the task. When routing a request fails for any other reason, its reply has a **Try again** button.

title: A task stopped when Ringkeeper restarted
text: A restart or an update stops tasks that were running. They say "Ringkeeper restarted during this task" and are listed on Home under **Cut short by a restart** for three days. **Resume** picks a task up where it stopped (one that hadn't got going starts over), and **Resume all** does them all. Sending a follow-up in the task's conversation works too.

title: A connection's test fails
text: Open the connection and press **Test connection** to see the service's own message. Usually the key was revoked or expired: paste a new one. A database must be reachable from this computer (not `localhost` on another machine), and Ringkeeper never connects to addresses on this computer itself.

title: A task went to the wrong project
text: Ringkeeper asks when it isn't sure, and remembers your answer for next time. Naming the project in the request ("in globex-portal") settles it. A project's other names (Clients & projects › the project) help too.

title: An approval disappeared
text: Held actions expire after 24 hours. The task says so, and you can ask it to try again. Activity shows what happened to each one.

title: A Google account stopped working
text: Its password changed (for mail), it was unused for six months, or its owner removed Ringkeeper. Open it under Connections and sign in again.

title: Where the logs are
text: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Ringkeeper\logs`: `backend.log` and `shell.log` (and the previous run's, `*.previous.log`). They never contain your keys.

title: Is it free?
text: Yes: free and open source (MIT). You pay Anthropic for Claude (your own API key, or your Claude subscription for personal use).

title: Does my clients' data go to you?
text: No. Ringkeeper runs on your computer, with no account and no server of ours. See Security for what leaves your computer, and where it goes.

title: Mac or Linux?
text: The desktop app is made for Windows 10 and 11. For Macs with macOS 12 or newer, Apple Silicon or Intel, there's an experimental unsigned build, reports welcome (how to install it). On Linux, the server install runs in Docker.

title: Why does Windows warn about the installer?
text: The beta isn't code-signed yet. Click **More info › Run anyway**.

title: Why won't my Mac open it?
text: The Mac build isn't signed yet. The first time, in Finder, choose **Go › Applications**, right-click **Ringkeeper**, and choose **Open**. See how to install it.

title: Where do I see what a task changed?
text: Open the task from Tasks: Data it changed lists what it did on connections, with Revert, and Changes shows its files.

title: Can a task run up a big bill?
text: Each task has a spending cap (Settings › Advanced, $1 by default). At the cap it pauses and asks whether to go on, with a Continue button. On a Claude subscription, which isn't billed per task, the cap is counted from the estimated cost.

title: Can it change things without asking?
text: Live client data never changes without asking. Reads always run. Changes on staging and development connections run and are logged. Changes on production connections, and anything that reaches real people (emails, texts), wait for your approval. See Approvals and safety.

title: Can I undo a change?
text: Database updates and deletes, Airtable records and n8n workflows: yes, for 7 days, from the task page. Sent emails, texts and deploys: no, and the approval says so first. See Undo.

title: What's the difference between an agent and a routine?
text: An agent is who does the work (its instructions and connections); a routine is when it runs (a schedule, an event, or Run now). See Agents and routines.

title: Can I approve from my phone?
text: Yes: Telegram, Slack or Discord. Safe changes can be approved there; risky ones say "Open in Ringkeeper". See Notifications.

title: How do I move to a new computer?
text: Make a backup in Settings › Backup and restore it on the new one. See Backup.

title: Can I use my Claude subscription instead of an API key?
text: For your own work, yes. Turn on Settings › Claude › Personal subscription mode, run `claude setup-token` in a terminal and paste the token, or use your Claude Code login. Your subscription is for your own use: use an API key for client work.

title: Where are my agents?
text: Agents in the menu lists every project's agents; the Agents tab on a project lists its own. **New agent** asks for the project first.

title: Is the desktop app a sandbox?
text: No. On the desktop, the AI runs as your Windows or Mac user. Ringkeeper's holds and gateway control what it does through connections, but it isn't a sandbox: a task can reach what your user can reach on this computer, including your files. For strong isolation, use server mode, where tasks run in Docker workers. See Security.

title: Can a task read scanned PDFs and pictures?
text: Yes, in the desktop app, after a one-time download. The first time a task meets a scan it can't read, the app offers the scan reader at the top of the window. If you choose Not now, it's in Settings › Reading scans. It reads English, on this computer, and nothing leaves it. On a Mac it needs macOS 15 or later. A server install doesn't read scans yet. Without the scan reader, a task can still look at a page as a picture, which keeps a table's or a chart's layout.

title: A task said it couldn't read a file, and ended as Not done. Why not Done?
text: Because what you asked for isn't there. When the main thing you asked for wasn't delivered, a task ends as Not done, even if it did part of it or suggests ways forward, so you can see at a glance that it needs you. Its answer names the file and what would work instead, like a PDF or .xlsx copy of a Numbers spreadsheet.

title: Something's wrong. Where do I start?
text: Troubleshooting, then Help › Report a problem in the app.

title: What Ringkeeper doesn't do yet
text: - **Isolation without Docker on the desktop:** tasks can't reach your own files only when they run in Docker (Settings > Security). Without Docker Desktop there's no separate account for tasks yet. - **Team accounts:** Ringkeeper is for one person; there are no teammates, shared logins or roles. - **A phone app:** there's no iPhone or Android app. Approve from Telegram, Slack or Discord; a server install also works in a phone's browser. - **Other languages:** the app is in English only, with no translations such as French or Spanish. Voice input understands other languages. - **Billing:** no invoices or time tracking. A client's month shows what their tasks cost and gives a report to send them (A client's month), but billing them is up to you. - **Exporting everything to spreadsheets:** a client's month downloads its tasks as CSV, and the Activity page its log. There's no export of all tasks at once, and a backup is a whole copy, for restoring.

title: Windows 10 and 11
text: Download `Ringkeeper_<version>_x64-setup.exe` from the latest release and run it. It installs for your user only: no administrator rights, nothing else to install, no terminal. Ringkeeper opens when it's done and walks you through first run; you need an Anthropic API key (platform.claude.com → API keys). **Windows may warn you first.** Until the installer is signed and well known, Microsoft Defender SmartScreen shows **"Windows protected your PC"**. Click **More info**, check that the app is `Ringkeeper_..._x64-setup.exe`, then click **Run anyway**. (If your browser flags the download, choose **Keep**.) If instead **Smart App Control** blocks it (some new Windows 11 PCs have it on), there's no "Run anyway": use a signed release once there is one. Turning Smart App Control off is possible in Windows Security, but it can't be turned back on without reinstalling Windows. - **Where things go:** the app in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Ringkeeper`, your data in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Ringkeeper` (the master key that protects your saved keys is in Windows Credential Manager), new projects in `Documents\Ringkeeper`. - **Updates:** Ringkeeper checks when it starts and every 6 hours (turn off **Check automatically** in Settings › About to check only when you ask), downloads updates in the background and shows **Update ready**. To check now, use **Check for updates** in Settings › About or the tray menu: it shows when it last checked, "You're up to date", the new version with its release notes and **Install and restart**, or what went wrong (offline, a signature that didn't verify). It never restarts by itself: while tasks run, the button is **Restart when tasks finish**. Once it's installed, the window opens again and says "Updated to" the new version, with a link to what's new, even if Ringkeeper had started at sign-in in the tray. It never touches your data, and if an update fails, the old version keeps working. - **Uninstall:** Settings → Apps → Ringkeeper → Uninstall. Your data stays unless you tick **Also delete my data**; your project folders always stay.

title: Mac, experimental
text: **Experimental and unsigned: reports welcome.** Each release also has two Mac downloads, for macOS 12 or newer. To see which is yours, open the Apple menu › **About This Mac**: - **Chip: Apple M1** or newer: `Ringkeeper_<version>_aarch64.dmg` - **Processor: Intel**: `Ringkeeper_<version>_x64.dmg` 1.
